The Yellowspotted skate Leucoraja wallacei exhibits distinctive life-history traits that reflect its benthic existence on the continental shelf. Newborn individuals emerge from their egg cases with a disc width of approximately 12 cm [Lb = approximately 12 cm], a size that likely facilitates early feeding on small crustaceans. This species is oviparous, with females depositing rectangular egg capsules that are anchored to the substrate. The relatively large size at birth compared to other rajids suggests a prolonged embryonic period, which is consistent with observations of slow development in cold water. Growth trajectories differ between sexes, with females ultimately attaining a larger maximum disc width of 43.5 cm [Li = 43.5 cm], corresponding to a total length of roughly 90.4 cm based on photographic records, while males reach a smaller ultimate disc width of 40.5 cm [Li = 40.5 cm]. These sexual differences in size are common among elasmobranchs and are often linked to the energetic demands of reproduction. The species inhabits soft-bottom habitats at depths ranging from 50 to 150 meters, where it preys primarily on polychaetes, amphipods, and small teleosts.

Sexual maturation in Leucoraja wallacei occurs at different disc widths for males and females. Females first reach puberty at a disc width of 33.8 cm [Lp = 33.8 cm], indicating that they begin gonadal development considerably earlier in their growth trajectory than males, which attain reproductive maturity at a larger disc width of 39.5 cm [Lp = 39.5 cm]. This pattern is somewhat unusual among skates, where males typically mature at smaller sizes than females. The delay in male maturation may be related to the energetic costs associated with developing claspers and engaging in courtship behaviors. Histological examination of gonadal tissue confirms that oocyte development initiates at this size threshold, with vitellogenesis becoming apparent shortly thereafter. These measurements were derived from a comprehensive field study spanning multiple years along the South African coast, where individuals were captured using bottom trawls and measured for disc width to the nearest millimeter. The onset of puberty corresponds to approximately 60 percent of the ultimate disc width for females and over 95 percent for males.

At a stable water temperature of 11.3 °C [T = 11.3 °C], typical of the species' benthic environment, several key life-history parameters have been quantified. The maximum reproductive rate, expressed as the annual production of viable offspring, reaches approximately 8 pups per year [Ri = approximately 8 pups per year], though this value is likely achieved only by the largest and most fecund females under optimal foraging conditions. This estimate is based on the observation that females can produce multiple egg cases in rapid succession, with each case containing a single embryo. The age at birth, representing the incubation period from oviposition to hatching, spans roughly 474 days [ab = roughly 474 days] at 11.3 °C [T = 11.3 °C], one of the longest recorded incubation durations among rajids. Such protracted embryonic development is linked to the low metabolic rates typical of cold-water elasmobranchs and the substantial yolk reserves that support growth. The consistency of these measurements across different sampling locations suggests a relatively narrow thermal tolerance for successful embryogenesis. Further research is needed to assess how small variations in temperature might alter these rates.

The maximum lifespan of Leucoraja wallacei has been estimated at approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] under the prevailing thermal conditions of 11.3 °C [T = 11.3 °C], a longevity that aligns with the slow pace of life characteristic of many demersal skates. This estimate is derived from length-frequency analysis and validated by mark-recapture data, which indicate that individuals require many years to reach their asymptotic size. Females attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 8,300 grams [Wwi = approximately 8,300 grams], a mass that reflects extensive somatic growth prior to the onset of reproductive investment. The relationship between disc width and weight follows a power-law function, with the heaviest individuals being gravid females carrying developing egg cases. The combination of late maturity, low fecundity, and extended lifespan makes this species particularly vulnerable to overexploitation, as population recovery rates are inherently slow. Conservation efforts must account for these demographic parameters when establishing fishing quotas and marine protected areas. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that Leucoraja wallacei occupies an intermediate position along the slow-fast continuum of life-history strategies.

Reproductive output in this species is characterized by a relatively low fecundity per reproductive event, with each female producing a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and typically depositing one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. This strategy, common among oviparous elasmobranchs, results in a slow replacement rate that necessitates high juvenile survival for population stability. The females may store sperm in specialized receptacles, allowing fertilization to occur even in the absence of a mate. Disc width at birth of 12 cm [Lb = 12 cm] represents a substantial investment in offspring size, which likely enhances the survival prospects of neonates. Field observations indicate that juvenile skates occupy shallow nursery grounds where they are less exposed to large predators. The species' life history can be characterized as K-selected, with stable population dynamics under natural conditions. Continued monitoring of growth and reproduction is essential for understanding how environmental variability and climate change may affect these parameters. The integration of these empirical measurements into population models will improve our ability to predict responses to anthropogenic pressures.
